categories.name: Coding Agents & AI IDEs

tools.name: Claude Code
tools.use: Terminal-based agent for multi-file changes in real repos
tools.why: Give it a task in plain English and it reads your whole project and makes the changes itself.

tools.name: Cursor
tools.use: AI-first code editor for building and refactoring whole apps
tools.why: A code editor with AI built in. You type what you want changed and it edits your project for you.

tools.name: OpenAI Codex
tools.use: Delegating coding tasks to a cloud or CLI agent
tools.why: ChatGPT's coding agent. Hand it a job and it works through it in the background.

tools.name: GitHub Copilot
tools.use: Inline completions and agent mode inside VS Code and GitHub
tools.why: Suggests the next lines of code as you type, so it's a gentle way to start using AI for coding.

tools.name: OpenCode
tools.use: Open-source coding agent that works with any AI model
tools.why: Free, open-source coding helper for your terminal, desktop or editor. Bring any AI model you already pay for (or use its free ones), so you're never locked into one company.

tools.name: Google Antigravity
tools.use: Google's agent-first coding app and CLI
tools.why: Google's coding app where AI agents plan, write and test code for you. The free plan has weekly limits; a Google AI plan gives more.

tools.name: Devin Desktop (formerly Windsurf)
tools.use: Agentic IDE for running and managing local and cloud coding agents
tools.why: An AI code editor that can take on bigger multi-step jobs across your project with little hand-holding.

tools.name: Grok Build
tools.use: Terminal-based coding agent from xAI
tools.why: Works like Claude Code: give it a task in plain English and it plans, edits your project and runs commands. Newer than the others here. A little use is free, and the $8/month Plus plan gives more.

categories.beginner: An AI helper that writes and fixes code with you, like a programmer sitting next to you who never gets tired.

categories.name: App Builders

tools.name: Lovable
tools.use: Prompt-to-full-stack web app with Supabase integration
tools.why: Easiest place to start: describe your app and it builds a working version you can click around in minutes.

tools.name: Bolt.new
tools.use: In-browser prompt-to-app builds you can run and deploy
tools.why: Type an idea and get a working website or app right in your browser, nothing to install.

tools.name: v0
tools.use: Generating React/Next.js UI and apps from prompts
tools.why: Great for good-looking websites and pages. Describe the look and it builds it for you.

tools.name: Replit
tools.use: Cloud IDE with an agent that builds and hosts apps
tools.why: Build, run and publish an app all in one place in your browser, with an AI helper that does the coding.

categories.beginner: Describe what you want in plain English and these build a working app or website for you, no coding needed to start.

categories.name: Deploy & Hosting

tools.name: Vercel
tools.use: Deploying Next.js and frontend apps from Git
tools.why: One click to put your website online with a real link, and it's free for small sites.

tools.name: Netlify
tools.use: Static sites and Jamstack apps with simple deploys
tools.why: Drag and drop your site to get it live on the internet. Simple and free to start.

tools.name: Cloudflare Workers & Pages
tools.use: Free global hosting for static sites, plus Workers for server code
tools.why: Free, fast hosting from one of the biggest internet companies. Static files are free and unlimited, and the free plan covers 100,000 server requests a day. Cloudflare now points new projects to Workers.

tools.name: Railway
tools.use: Deploying backends, workers, and databases with little config
tools.why: Puts apps that need a server or database online without you managing any computers.

tools.name: Render
tools.use: Hosting web services, cron jobs, and Postgres
tools.why: A simple place to run your app and its database online, with a free tier to try it.

categories.beginner: Where your website or app lives on the internet so anyone can visit it with a link.

categories.name: Auth

tools.name: Clerk
tools.use: Drop-in sign-in UI and user management for React/Next.js
tools.why: Adds polished sign-up and log-in screens to your app in minutes.

tools.name: Supabase Auth
tools.use: Auth bundled with your Supabase Postgres database
tools.why: Free log-ins that come bundled with Supabase, so your accounts and data live in one place.

tools.name: Better Auth
tools.use: Free, open-source auth that keeps users in your own database
tools.why: A free log-in system you add to your own code, so your users and passwords live in your own database. It took over from NextAuth (Auth.js). An optional hosted dashboard with logs and security alerts is free to start, then $20/month on Pro.

tools.name: Auth0
tools.use: Enterprise-grade auth, SSO, and identity
tools.why: Battle-tested log-in system that big companies trust when security really matters.

tools.name: Firebase Authentication
tools.use: Simple auth for mobile and web apps on Google's stack
tools.why: Google's free log-in system, with easy 'Sign in with Google' and phone login.

categories.beginner: Handles sign-up, log-in and passwords so your users can have accounts without you building it from scratch.

categories.name: Payments & Email
categories.beginner: Tools that let your site take money and send emails like receipts, sign-up confirmations and password resets, without you building any of it yourself.

tools.name: Stripe
tools.use: Accept card payments, subscriptions and checkout links
tools.why: The standard way to take payments online. Make a payment link with no code, or add checkout to your app. No monthly fee: 2.9% + 30¢ per US card sale.

tools.name: Resend
tools.use: Send emails from your app: receipts, sign-ups, password resets
tools.why: The easiest way for an app to send emails, and AI coding tools know it well. Free for 3,000 emails a month (100 a day); $20/month for 50,000.

tools.name: Paddle
tools.use: Sell software and subscriptions with sales tax handled for you
tools.why: Paddle becomes the official seller, so it collects and files sales tax and VAT worldwide for you. No monthly fee: 5% + 50¢ per sale.

tools.name: Polar
tools.use: Sell digital products, licenses and subscriptions, tax handled
tools.why: Like Paddle but made for developers and indie makers, with clear posted prices. Free to start at 5% + 50¢ per sale, with lower rates on paid plans as you grow.

tools.name: Postmark
tools.use: Reliable transactional email for important messages
tools.why: Known for getting important emails like password resets into the inbox fast. The free plan is 100 emails a month for testing; paid plans start at $15/month for 10,000.

categories.name: Databases & Backend

tools.name: Supabase
tools.use: Postgres, auth, storage, and realtime in one backend
tools.why: Stores your app's data plus log-ins and file uploads, all in one free-to-start package.

tools.name: Firebase
tools.use: Realtime NoSQL backend for quick mobile/web apps
tools.why: Google's all-in-one backend for saving data, great for phone apps and realtime updates.

tools.name: Neon
tools.use: Serverless Postgres with branching
tools.why: A simple online database that's free to start and only charges when it's actually being used.

tools.name: Convex
tools.use: Reactive TypeScript backend with built-in database
tools.why: A backend where your app's data updates live on screen, without setting up servers.

tools.name: PlanetScale
tools.use: Scalable managed MySQL/Postgres
tools.why: A heavy-duty database for when your app gets lots of users and needs to stay fast.

categories.beginner: The place your app saves its information, like customers, orders or jobs, so nothing gets lost.

categories.name: Design-to-Code

tools.name: Figma Make
tools.use: Turning prompts and Figma designs into working prototypes
tools.why: Sketch or describe a screen and it turns it into a working prototype you can click.

tools.name: Builder.io
tools.use: Converting Figma designs into framework code
tools.why: Turns designs into real web pages and lets you edit the site visually, like a page builder.

tools.name: Locofy
tools.use: Figma/Penpot to React, Next.js, and mobile code
tools.why: Converts your Figma designs into real app or website code.

tools.name: Anima
tools.use: Exporting Figma designs to React/HTML code
tools.why: Takes a design from Figma and turns it into a working website.

categories.beginner: Turns a picture or mockup of how your app should look into a real, clickable screen.

categories.name: Testing & QA

tools.name: Playwright
tools.use: Reliable end-to-end browser tests (open source)
tools.why: Free tool that clicks through your site like a real person to catch anything that breaks.

tools.name: Cypress
tools.use: Developer-friendly E2E and component testing
tools.why: Lets you watch automated tests click through your app so you can see exactly where bugs happen.

tools.name: Sentry
tools.use: Catching errors and crashes in production
tools.why: Emails you when your live app crashes and shows exactly what went wrong.

categories.beginner: Tools that check your app for bugs and broken buttons before your customers find them.

categories.name: AI Code Review
categories.beginner: An AI that reads every change to your code before it goes live and points out bugs, security holes and sloppy mistakes, like a second pair of eyes that never gets tired.

tools.name: CodeRabbit
tools.use: AI code review on pull requests
tools.why: An AI reviewer that reads your code changes and points out bugs before they go live. Free for public projects; paid plans start at $24 per developer a month (billed yearly).

tools.name: Greptile
tools.use: AI code review that understands your whole codebase
tools.why: Reviews each change with your whole project in mind, so it catches bugs that only show up across files, with less noise. Free for one developer (50 reviews' worth of credits a month); Pro has no seat fees: you prepay credits at $1 each (a basic review uses 1 credit), shared across your team.

tools.name: Cursor Bugbot
tools.use: Automatic AI review on GitHub pull requests
tools.why: Cursor's reviewer checks every GitHub pull request for real logic bugs and lets you fix them in one click. Billed from your Cursor plan's usage, about $1 to $1.50 per review.

categories.name: LLM APIs

tools.name: OpenAI API
tools.use: General-purpose GPT models for chat, tools, and vision
tools.why: The ChatGPT brain you can plug into your own app or chatbot.

tools.name: Anthropic API
tools.use: Claude models, strong at coding and long context
tools.why: Claude's brain for your own app. Great at writing, reasoning and long documents.

tools.name: Google Gemini API
tools.use: Gemini models with large context and multimodal input
tools.why: Google's AI with a generous free tier, good for chatbots and reading images or PDFs.

tools.name: xAI API
tools.use: Grok models plus image, video and voice on one API key
tools.why: Grok's AI for your own app. The same key also makes images, video and voice, and it can search the web and X live. Pay as you go, with a free playground to test before you buy.

tools.name: DeepSeek API
tools.use: Low-cost models with OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs
tools.why: Very cheap AI for your own app, and it works with code written for OpenAI or Claude. Pay as you go with no free tier, and prices drop by half outside peak hours.

tools.name: OpenRouter
tools.use: One API key to route across many model providers
tools.why: One account to try many different AI models and pick the best price for your chatbot.

categories.beginner: The AI 'brains' you plug into your own app to make it chat, write, answer questions or read documents.

categories.name: AI Images & Art
categories.beginner: Tools that make pictures from a sentence you type. Describe what you want, like "a cute cartoon cat emote waving", and they draw it in seconds. Great for emotes, stickers, logos, thumbnails, avatars and art for games.

tools.name: ChatGPT Images
tools.use: Quick images and edits by chatting
tools.why: Just describe the picture in plain English and ask for changes like "make it smaller and add a blue outline". Easiest place to start.

tools.name: Nano Banana (Gemini)
tools.use: Make and edit images by chatting in the Gemini app
tools.why: Google's image maker inside Gemini. Great at editing your own photos, keeping a character looking the same, and putting clear words in pictures. Free to use; a Google AI plan unlocks the best model and higher limits.

tools.name: Midjourney
tools.use: High-quality illustrations and artistic images
tools.why: Produces some of the most beautiful, artistic images around. No free plan, so try a free option first.

tools.name: FLUX (Black Forest Labs)
tools.use: Photo-real images and an image API with open models
tools.why: Makes very realistic photos and product shots, and it's one of the cheapest to use in your own app (pay per image, no subscription). Some versions are free to download and run on a powerful computer.

tools.name: Ideogram
tools.use: Logos, stickers, posters and images with readable text
tools.why: The best at putting real, readable words inside a picture, so it's great for logos, thumbnails and channel art. Free credits every week.

tools.name: Grok Imagine
tools.use: Quick images from a sentence, right inside Grok
tools.why: Type what you want and it makes pictures in seconds, then you can ask for changes. The free plan includes a limited number of images a day (xAI doesn't say how many).

tools.name: Recraft
tools.use: Logos, icons, vector art and brand sets
tools.why: Makes clean logos and icons that stay sharp at any size, so they look good as tiny emotes and on big banners alike.

tools.name: Leonardo
tools.use: Emotes, game assets, characters and stylized art
tools.why: Lots of ready-made art styles for cartoons, game items and characters, which makes it easy to get a consistent look for a set of emotes. Free tokens every day.

categories.name: AI Audio & Voice
categories.beginner: Tools that make sound for you. Type a description or a script and they create music, jingles, realistic voiceovers, or clean up and transcribe your recordings. Great for podcasts, YouTube and stream intros.

tools.name: Suno
tools.use: Songs, jingles and background music from a text description
tools.why: Describe the song you want, like "upbeat 10-second podcast intro jingle", and it makes it with music and even vocals. Free to try; downloading and commercial use need the $10/mo plan.

tools.name: ElevenLabs
tools.use: Realistic AI voiceovers, narration, sound effects and music
tools.why: Paste your script and it reads it out in a natural human-sounding voice. Also makes sound effects. Free monthly credits, paid from $6/mo.

tools.name: Descript
tools.use: Edit podcasts and videos by editing the transcript
tools.why: Turns your recording into text, and you edit the audio just like a document: delete a word and it's gone from the recording. Free plan includes 60 minutes a month.

categories.name: AI for Hardware & Electronics
categories.beginner: Tools for projects you can touch: Arduino, ESP32 and Raspberry Pi boards, sensors, wiring, robots, 3D printing and smart-home gadgets. They help you write the code for your board, test your wiring safely on screen before you plug anything in, and even design your own circuit boards.

tools.name: Arduino Cloud
tools.use: Write, upload and control Arduino/ESP32 projects with a built-in AI assistant
tools.why: Arduino's own online editor has an AI helper that writes and fixes the code for your board, and lets you control wireless (Wi-Fi) projects from your phone. Free plan includes 30 AI requests a month.

tools.name: Wokwi
tools.use: Simulate Arduino, ESP32 and Raspberry Pi Pico projects in your browser
tools.why: Build and test your circuit on screen with virtual boards, sensors and LEDs, including Wi-Fi on the ESP32, so you can't fry real parts while learning. Free for public projects.

tools.name: Tinkercad
tools.use: Beginner circuits and 3D-printable designs
tools.why: Autodesk's free, super-friendly tool for designing parts to 3D print and wiring up practice circuits with a virtual Arduino.

tools.name: ChatGPT
tools.use: Explain wiring, write firmware and troubleshoot step by step
tools.why: Describe your parts and what you want them to do and it explains the wiring and writes the board code. You can even send it a photo of your setup when something isn't working.

tools.name: Flux
tools.use: AI-assisted circuit and PCB design
tools.why: An AI helper for designing your own custom circuit board, from parts list to a board you can order. Paid after a 14-day free trial (free for students).

tools.name: OpenPLC
tools.use: Free, open-source PLC you can program with ladder logic
tools.why: Learn and test PLC programs (ladder logic, structured text) for free without buying an industrial controller. It can run on a regular PC or a Raspberry Pi.

categories.name: AI Video & Clips
categories.beginner: Tools for short videos: TikToks, Reels, YouTube Shorts and stream highlights. They cut long videos into clips, add captions automatically and help you edit without learning pro software.

tools.name: CapCut
tools.use: Edit shorts and reels with auto captions
tools.why: A free, easy video editor made for TikTok-style videos. Auto captions, templates and simple cuts are on the free plan; some effects need Pro.

tools.name: Opus Clip
tools.use: Turn a long video or stream into short clips
tools.why: Upload a long video or paste a YouTube link and AI picks the best moments, crops them vertical and adds captions. Free plan gives 60 minutes of video a month, with a watermark.

tools.name: Gemini Omni (formerly Veo)
tools.use: Realistic AI video clips with sound, made and edited by chatting
tools.why: Google's video maker in the Gemini app, which replaced Veo. Describe a scene or upload photos and it makes a realistic clip with sound, then you can ask for changes. Needs a paid Google AI plan.

tools.name: Kling AI
tools.use: Make AI video clips from text or a picture
tools.why: Makes smooth, realistic clips with good lip-sync at a low price. The free plan lets you try it (watermarked, personal use only), and paid plans start under $10 a month.

tools.name: Descript
tools.use: Edit video by editing the transcript
tools.why: Your video becomes a text document. Delete words in the text and they're cut from the video. Good for talking videos and podcasts.

tools.name: Runway
tools.use: Generate short AI video clips from text or images
tools.why: Makes brand-new video clips from a description or a picture. Free plan is a one-time 125 credits, enough to try a few clips.

tools.name: Grok Imagine
tools.use: Short AI video clips with sound from text or a picture
tools.why: Turns a description or a picture into a short clip with sound effects and even talking characters. Video needs the $30/month Premium plan, so try Runway's free credits first.

categories.name: Automations & Agents
categories.beginner: Tools that connect your apps so boring tasks happen on their own, like sending new form signups to a spreadsheet or emailing you when an order comes in. No coding needed.

tools.name: Zapier
tools.use: Connect apps with simple if-this-then-that steps
tools.why: The easiest place to start: pick a trigger and an action and it just runs. Free plan covers 100 tasks a month with two-step automations.

tools.name: Make
tools.use: Visual drag-and-drop automations
tools.why: Draw your automation as a flowchart. More free room than Zapier (1,000 credits a month), a little more to learn.

tools.name: n8n
tools.use: Powerful automations and AI agents you can host yourself
tools.why: Very flexible and free if you run it on your own computer or server. The hosted version is a 14-day trial, then paid. Best once you're comfortable.

tools.name: Grok Bot
tools.use: AI teammates that work in your apps and run routines on a schedule
tools.why: Instead of building a flowchart, you tell it the job in plain English and it signs into your tools and does it, even on a schedule. VibePicks is built and run with it. It starts at $30/month, and simple fixed tasks are cheaper and more predictable in Zapier or Make.

categories.name: Websites & Stores
categories.beginner: For a simple business website or online shop, like a bakery, a portfolio or selling your crafts. These build the site for you from templates or a prompt, and you edit by dragging things around. No coding, and no need for a full custom app.

tools.name: Wix
tools.use: AI-built business websites with drag-and-drop editing
tools.why: Describe your business and its AI builds a starter site you can then drag and edit. Free plan works but shows Wix ads and a wixsite.com address.

tools.name: Shopify
tools.use: Online store to sell products
tools.why: The standard for selling things online: products, checkout, shipping and payments in one place. Short free trial, then usually $1 a month for 3 months before regular pricing.

tools.name: Framer
tools.use: Good-looking sites and landing pages with AI layouts
tools.why: Great for a sharp-looking landing page or portfolio. AI can draft the layout for you. Free plan uses a Framer address and badge.

tools.name: Squarespace
tools.use: Polished templates for a simple business site or shop
tools.why: Clean, professional templates that are hard to make look bad. No free plan, but there's a 14-day free trial.

categories.name: Writing & Marketing
categories.beginner: Tools for the words around your project: social posts, emails, newsletters, product descriptions and ads. Tell them what you sell and who it's for, then edit the draft so it sounds like you.

tools.name: ChatGPT
tools.use: Draft posts, emails and product descriptions
tools.why: Tell it what you're selling and who it's for and it writes a first draft in seconds. Ask for a few versions and pick the one that sounds most like you.

tools.name: Claude
tools.use: Natural-sounding writing and rewrites
tools.why: Good at writing that doesn't sound like a robot, and at rewriting your own draft to be clearer. Free plan has daily limits.

tools.name: Gemini
tools.use: Drafts and rewrites, built into Gmail and Google Docs
tools.why: Google's AI assistant. Good for first drafts and rewrites, and handy if you live in Gmail and Google Docs, since paid plans put it right inside them. The free plan has everyday limits.

tools.name: Grok
tools.use: Timely social posts and replies
tools.why: A chat assistant like ChatGPT that can read live posts on X and the web, so it's handy for writing about what people are talking about today. The free plan has limited daily use; the $8/month Plus plan gives more.

tools.name: Grammarly
tools.use: Fix spelling, grammar and tone as you type
tools.why: Checks your writing everywhere you type, in email, social posts and docs. The free plan catches spelling and grammar mistakes.

categories.name: CAD & Machining
categories.beginner: Tools for designing real parts and making them on a 3D printer, CNC mill or lathe. Honest note: most CAD and CAM is not AI yet. A few tools now let you describe a part in words, and AI chat can help explain G-code, but always check toolpaths and simulate before you cut metal.

tools.name: Fusion
tools.use: CAD and CAM in one, from design to toolpaths
tools.why: Design the part and make the toolpaths in the same program. Free for personal, non-commercial use (under $1,000 a year), with limits like 10 active designs and 3-axis CAM. Its AI Assistant is still a preview, and generative design needs a paid plan.

tools.name: Onshape
tools.use: Browser-based CAD that runs on any computer
tools.why: Full 3D CAD in your web browser, no install. Free plan, but your designs are public. Includes an AI Advisor that answers how-to questions.

tools.name: Zoo Zookeeper
tools.use: Describe a part in words and get an editable 3D CAD model
tools.why: Type something like "a flange with 4 bolt holes" and it makes an editable CAD model you can export as STEP. Works best on simple parts. Free plan includes $10 of AI use a month.

tools.name: Tinkercad
tools.use: Very simple 3D designs for printing
tools.why: Autodesk's free beginner tool. Not AI, but the easiest way to make a 3D-printable part in an afternoon.

tools.name: ChatGPT
tools.use: Explain and draft G-code, feeds and speeds
tools.why: Good for learning what G-code lines do or drafting a simple program from your dimensions and tool. It can get things wrong, so always simulate and dry-run above the part before cutting.

releases.title: Supabase Compute is in private alpha: run AI agents, background jobs and APIs (Node, Deno or any Dockerfile) inside your Supabase project, next to your Postgres data, for minutes or hours instead of the 400-second Edge Function limit. Deploy with supabase compute push (CLI v2.120.0+); free during the alpha, us-west-2 projects only, waitlist required and not for production yet

Replit Cloud Agents let anyone on a team describe a change in plain English, watch it in a live preview of the running app, and have the agent open a tested pull request on GitHub (or merge request on GitLab) that follows the team's guidelines and keeps fixing it as review comments come in. Engineers still approve what ships. Available now on Pro and Enterprise
Cursor design mode adds Annotate: give the agent visual prompts by editing elements, drawing right on the page, and reviewing your design at different screen sizes

Google released the Gemini API CLI (gemini-api) in beta, a stateless, zero-dependency command-line client built for AI coding agents, scripts and CI pipelines. It uses the Interactions API to generate text and media, analyze files and run Gemini managed agents

Ramp opened early access to Inspect, the cloud coding agent its own teams use: hand it a task from Slack, GitHub, Linear, the web or your phone (even a screenshot with "@inspect fix this") and it returns a visually checked, reviewed pull request. Sessions are multiplayer so teammates can jump in and steer. Ramp says it now writes 74% of the company's merged PRs

Vercel Observability now shows AI traffic: requests by each verified AI bot, the pages AI crawlers hit most, pages AI assistants fetch in answer to a user's question, Markdown requests, and pages that return errors to bots. Find it under Observability > AI Traffic; querying it from the CLI with vercel metrics needs Observability Plus

OpenCode v2.2.0 adds experimental desktop plugins you can create, install and share, a refreshed desktop app, experimental image-generation APIs for plugins, keyed session instructions that survive compaction without busting the prompt cache, and prompt-cache lifetimes you can set per provider and model. Heads-up: the OpenCode GitHub Action is no longer published, so remove it from your workflows

OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra, a fast, lower-cost model for computer use, visual reasoning and writing. On the API as gpt-6.1-terra at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output (half the price of GPT-6.1 Sol), with a 1M-token context; also in ChatGPT and Codex for paid plans, and generally available in GitHub Copilot

Cursor's Agent SDK is generally available: define an agent as a folder (instructions.md for the prompt, tools/ in TypeScript, skills, MCP connections), test it with built-in evals, and deploy it to Cursor with agent-sdk deploy or run it on your own servers. Agents can wake on GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket events, Slack messages, webhooks or a schedule

Assisted permissions are generally available in Copilot CLI, the Copilot app and VS Code: an AI model checks each command, file path or URL Copilot asks to use, lets clearly safe ones run, and still asks you about the rest. It's a middle ground between approving everything by hand and Allow All

v2.1.311 fixes long sessions stopping with "Usage credits required for 1M context" past 200K tokens (it now compacts and keeps going), fixes multi-thousand-line edits stalling for up to 5 seconds, lets subagents use MCP servers that connect late, and typing ultrathink mid-turn now raises effort for the rest of that turn

Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke's Entire launched a Git hosting platform built for coding agents: Trails replace pull requests with agent-scored checks on every push, Continuous Memory saves agent sessions into the repo so agents can search past work, and Buildkite and Depot handle CI. Open to every developer today, with private repos only for now
New paid-tier projects now store Generate Content API requests by default (store=true), matching the Interactions API; opt out per request with store=false or in Logs and Datasets settings
Faster pnpm installs: dependency verification is reused across deployments, cutting average install time 14% on Pro, automatic on all plans
Replit now works fully in Japanese, from the interface to prompts and agent output

Cloudflare added two emergency Managed Ruleset rules for the Node.js Brotli decoder flaw CVE-2026-111497 (memory leak or code execution when decoding attacker-controlled Brotli data): one matches Brotli-encoded request bodies, one matches the Next.js image optimizer path /_next/image. Both default to Log, not Block. If you self-host Next.js or any Node app, upgrade Node.js to 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1

Vercel Connect can now create a separate restricted Stripe API key for each agent or task (Managed API Key method), limited to the permissions you pick, so an agent never holds your full-access secret key. Vercel stores the key, and you can rotate it without redeploying

The new GitHub app for Microsoft Teams combines notifications with Copilot: @mention GitHub on a bug report in a channel or chat and it investigates, fixes the bug and opens a pull request for review. The legacy app is renamed GitHub (deprecated) and retires November 16

Cursor agents can now control your computer: Computer Use lets them click and type across desktop apps, not just the browser, such as driving the iOS Simulator to test the features they build. Cursor uses it on its own when a task needs it, or you can @-mention Computer Use; update Cursor to get it

Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro, a 2.8T-parameter MoE model (104B active) with a 1M-token context and image input, aimed at full-project coding and long agent runs. It is live on the Kimi API and Vercel AI Gateway (moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro, plus a faster Highspeed version), with open weights planned by November 4

Replit launched Monitoring Agent, an on-call agent that investigates production issues from your app's logs and metrics, then attempts and validates fixes (with optional auto-fix and experimental auto-republish). Also new: Agent-made reusable skills, chat and asset sharing, Stripe Atlas incorporation at 20% off, and published apps that keep running at zero credits for eligible top-up customers

Chroma, the open-source vector database, signed a deal to join Replit. Chroma Cloud is winding down: writes stop November 22, 2026 and reads stop December 22, 2026, so cloud users need to export and migrate. Open-source ChromaDB stays Apache 2.0

Codex CLI 0.164.0 lets you save reusable prompts and slash commands in ten numbered /presets slots, set the model and permissions inline with /model and /permissions, preview images in the terminal, and mask credentials in remote Bash commands

TanStack AI hits 1.0 with stable core APIs: an open-source, no-lock-in toolkit for adding chat, tools, MCP, media and agents to your app, with 23 provider adapters, eight UI frameworks and a new experimental agent harness

You can now deploy to Vercel without an account: run vercel deploy --temporary (or point it at a single file) to get a shareable tmp.now URL for a prototype. Temporary deployments expire after one hour unless you open the claim link and sign in

You can now self-host Amp orbs: run amp orb provider on your own machines (Docker, E2B, Modal, Vercel Sandbox, Daytona or Kubernetes) so agents run inside your own network; free for individuals and teams, and free for every workspace until Oct 29

Anthropic donated Agent Skills, the open SKILL.md standard used by 70+ agent platforms including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and VS Code, to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, so skills you write stay vendor-neutral

The Decisions API is now generally available: you define a question and its allowed answers and get fast, low-cost classification, routing and next-action picks for apps and agents, up to 10x faster than GPT-6 Luna through the Responses API, now with prompt caching, JSON and image inputs and up to 400 questions per request

Agents SDK v0.30.0 runs PiHarness on Pi 1.4, so agents can hibernate while tasks sleep, park tasks that keep crashing, and recover from storage errors and cut-off model streams; the upgrade can't be rolled back past Pi 1.4

Recursive released Flint, a free Apache 2.0 coding model that runs on a laptop (40B mixture-of-experts, about 2.5B active), downloadable on Hugging Face so you can code offline and keep your code private

GemDB launched GemDB Code, a free VS Code extension where your code is the database schema, so a coding agent can change objects without writing migrations; Python only at launch, with a built-in MCP server for plain-English data questions

New createAI function in the agents package gives the AI SDK one provider for Workers AI models, AI Gateway catalog models, dynamic routes and vendor models, with fallbacks, caching and stream resume; workers-ai-provider and ai-gateway-provider are now deprecated

You can now choose 12-hour prompt caching in the Responses API, so shared instructions, tools and context stay cached at the lower cached-input rate even when requests are hours apart; 12-hour cache writes cost 2.5x the input token price

WebSocket support in Vercel Functions is now generally available, for AI chat, streaming and realtime multiplayer apps, at the same limits and pricing as other Function invocations (CPU billed only while processing messages)
Your coding agent can now query your Supabase logs, and a new Supabase skill points it to the signals to watch: error spikes, security issues, slow queries and growing usage, on a schedule you choose

v2.1.304 adds /auto-mode-setup, a guided setup that reads your project and recent sessions to teach auto mode about your setup, warns Pro and Max users when resuming an old conversation would use a noticeable share of their 5-hour limit, and fixes claude --worktree deleting a worktree and its branch at exit without asking, which could lose commits

Inception's Mercury 3, a diffusion LLM that writes 1,000+ tokens per second with a 1M-token context, is live on Inception's OpenAI-compatible API (new keys get 100M free tokens) and on OpenRouter, Baseten and Vercel AI Gateway; launch price is $0.10/$0.35 per million tokens, 50% off its $0.20/$0.70 list price

Clairic, a new extraction model in preview on Workers AI (@cf/cloudflare/clairic), pulls typed values like invoice totals, dates and lists out of text or up to four images, with a confidence score on every answer, for $0.10 per million input tokens and no output charge; open weights are planned

MiniMax's new fast model for coding, agent work and visual reasoning (74% on DeepSWE) is live on the MiniMax API at a flat $0.15/$0.60 per million tokens, about 1/3 the cost of M3 at 3x the speed; open weights arrive Oct 23
AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests by conversation and shows which coding agent ran it (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor), plus its cost, models and cache hit rate
OpenAI is now the preferred partner powering Replit Agent's default experience, CEO Amjad Masad says; Replit stays model-agnostic, so you can still pick Anthropic's Claude and other supported models
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 now powers the deepseek-flash API model (open weights on Hugging Face), and DeepSeek's Search and Fetch web APIs are open to all developers at $0.75 per 1,000 calls

v2.1.302 turns on fork subagents by default in claude -p, the Agent SDK, the desktop app and VS Code (CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 turns them off), adds an idle-compaction toggle in /config, and warns that standalone Claude Design (claude.ai/design) closes by December 14, 2026

You can now see and control your macOS or Linux runner's desktop from Amp, handy for trying native apps (like iOS apps) that Amp builds for you; turn on Share This Mac's Display or run amp --no-tui --desktop

New visual-reasoning model that keeps re-checking images and video while it thinks (it can crop, pull frames and run code); research preview with API access at $0.60/$3 per million tokens, also on OpenRouter

ChatGPT Slides: build a deck from a chat, files or an outline, edit it with teammates in real time, present from ChatGPT, or export to PowerPoint, PDF or Google Slides; rolling out to Pro, Business and Enterprise users with Space access

Beam, a 501B-parameter (23B active) open-weight model for coding and agents, is out under Apache 2.0 with the open-source Mirror CLI; free to start on Reflection's API and also on OpenRouter, Vercel, Ollama and other partners
Cloud agents can now build interactive canvases (dashboards, reports) you share with a link; Environments API in beta; cloud environments now hold up to 300 repos and large ones load 5x faster
JetBrains' free on-device coding agent runs on NVIDIA RTX Spark at launch, and Windows support is now stable on RTX cards with 24 GB+ VRAM: no token bill, and your code never leaves the machine
Google AI Pro subscribers can now build apps with Gemini 4 Argon in AI Studio Build and the playground
HeyGen Video 1, its video generation model, is now available in the HeyGen MCP server, so you can ask your AI agent for a video and get it back in seconds
New Agents section in your Clerk app config with setup for adding auth to your MCP server, plus a ready-made agent prompt for building a new MCP server

Code Review is generally available on Claude Team and Enterprise: automatic reviews on new GitHub pull requests, about 3x faster than the preview (6-10 minutes), with Quick, Standard or Deep review levels per repo
Fast mode for Claude Opus 5.5 is out of research preview: up to 2.5x faster output, no waitlist or beta header, $8/$40 per million tokens
Neon Realtime in public beta: subscribe to any read-only SQL query and your app updates live, with React hooks and a coding-agent skill; free during beta
Code layers enter open beta (code-backed prototypes on the canvas, all plans), plus Specs for Markdown context you can hand to coding agents via Figma MCP
Open 120B Nemotron 3.5 Super VL (text, image, video; up to 1M context) and Bolt 74B-A9B, a local agent model that fits in 24GB; on Hugging Face and OpenRouter
Open-weights 5.6B image model with native 4K and up to 10 reference images; runs on consumer GPUs, API from $0.009 per 1K image
New image editing model: most edits under 8 seconds at native 2K, keeps products and characters consistent; $0.06 per 2K image, also on fal, Replicate and OpenRouter
Bluesky's Attie now lets anyone describe and build small shareable sites, games, quizzes and polls with no code, with Bluesky sign-in built in
Open-weight version of Muse Spark for self-hosted agentic coding, 1M context
Google's newest frontier model is now available to developers via the paid Gemini API tier and AI Studio
Gemini 4 Argon now generally available in Copilot (Pro+, Max, Business, Enterprise)
New model on Muse Code and Meta Model API at $4/$20 per million tokens
